You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

Also formats your code (no need to use `gofmt` or `goimports` separately). ## Features - Sort imports into logical groups (stdlib, general, company, project) - Remove unused imports with `-rm-unused` - Set aliases for versioned packages with `-set-alias` - Format code automatically with `-format` - Apply to directories recursively - Group company imports separately with `-company-prefixes` ## Usage ### Basic command: ```bash goimports-reviser -rm-unused -set-alias -format ./reviser/reviser.go ``` ### Apply to a directory recursively: ```bash goimports-reviser -rm-unused -set-alias -format -recursive reviser ``` ### Apply to all files: ```bash goimports-reviser -rm-unused -set-alias -format ./... ``` ### Apply to multiple targets: ```bash goimports-reviser -rm-unused -set-alias -format ./reviser/reviser.go ./pkg/... ``` ### Options: ```text Usage of goimports-reviser: -apply-to-generated-files Apply imports sorting and formatting(if the option is set) to generated files. Generated file is a file with first comment which starts with comment '// Code generated'. Optional parameter. -company-prefixes string Company package prefixes which will be placed after 3rd-party group by default(if defined). Values should be comma-separated. Optional parameters. -excludes string Exclude files or dirs, example: '.git/,proto/*.go'. -file-path string Deprecated. Put file name as an argument(last item) of command line. -format Option will perform additional formatting. Optional parameter. -imports-order string Your imports groups can be sorted in your way. std - std import group; general - libs for general purpose; company - inter-org or your company libs(if you set '-company-prefixes'-option, then 4th group will be split separately. In other case, it will be the part of general purpose libs); project - your local project dependencies; blanked - imports with "_" alias; dotted - imports with "." alias. Optional parameter. (default "std,general,company,project") -list-diff Option will list files whose formatting differs from goimports-reviser. Optional parameter. -local string Deprecated -output string Can be "file", "write" or "stdout". Whether to write the formatted content back to the file or to stdout. When "write" together with "-list-diff" will list the file name and write back to the file. Optional parameter. (default "file") -project-name string Your project name(ex.: github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser). Optional parameter. -recursive Apply rules recursively if target is a directory. In case of ./... execution will be recursively applied by default. Optional parameter. -rm-unused Remove unused imports. Optional parameter. -separate-named Separate named imports from their group with a new line. Optional parameter. -set-alias Set alias for versioned package names, like 'github.com/go-pg/pg/v9'. In this case import will be set as 'pg "github.com/go-pg/pg/v9"'. Optional parameter. -set-exit-status set the exit status to 1 if a change is needed/made. Optional parameter. -use-cache Use cache to improve performance. Optional parameter. -version Show version. ``` ## Examples ### Before usage: ```go package testdata import ( "log" "github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/testdata/innderpkg" "bytes" "golang.org/x/exp/slices" ) ``` ### After usage: ```go package testdata import ( "bytes" "log" "golang.org/x/exp/slices" "github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/testdata/innderpkg" ) ``` Comments for imports are preserved: ```go package testdata import ( "fmt" // comments to the package here ) ``` ### Example with `-company-prefixes` option Before: ```go package testdata // goimports-reviser/testdata import ( "fmt" //fmt package "golang.org/x/exp/slices" //custom package "github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/pkg" // this is a company package which is not a part of the project, but is a part of your organization "goimports-reviser/pkg" ) ``` After: ```go package testdata // goimports-reviser/testdata import ( "fmt" // fmt package "golang.org/x/exp/slices" // custom package "github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/pkg" // this is a company package which is not a part of the project, but is a part of your organization "goimports-reviser/pkg" ) ``` ### Example with `-imports-order std,general,company,project,blanked,dotted` option Before: ```go package testdata // goimports-reviser/testdata import ( _ "github.com/pkg1" . "github.com/pkg2" "fmt" //fmt package "golang.org/x/exp/slices" //custom package "github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/pkg" // this is a company package which is not a part of the project, but is a part of your organization "goimports-reviser/pkg" ) ``` After: ```go package testdata // goimports-reviser/testdata import ( "fmt" // fmt package "golang.org/x/exp/slices" // custom package "github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/pkg" // this is a company package which is not a part of the project, but is a part of your organization "goimports-reviser/pkg" _ "github.com/pkg1" . "github.com/pkg2" ) ``` ### Example with `-format` option Before: ```go package main func test(){ } func additionalTest(){ } ``` After: ```go package main func test(){ } func additionalTest(){ } ``` ### Example with `-separate-named` option Before: ```go package testdata // goimports-reviser/testdata import ( "fmt" "github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/pkg" extpkg "google.com/golang/pkg" "golang.org/x/exp/slices" extslice "github.com/PeterRK/slices" ) ``` After: ```go package testdata // goimports-reviser/testdata import ( "fmt" "github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/pkg" "golang.org/x/exp/slices" extpkg "google.com/golang/pkg" extslice "github.com/PeterRK/slices" ) ```

# Interesting differences:
# Without -format: 
#   - const a/b are together (no blank line)
#   - type T{} has blank line before/after
#   - func test/test2 have no blank line between them
# With -format:
#   - const a/b have blank line between them
#   - func test/test2 have blank line between them

# The -format option seems to use a different printer that adds blank lines
# between all top-level declarations.

# This is actually goimports's "source" mode which uses go/printer with more options
# Let me look at what goimports does differently

# Let me check if there's a different set of printer flags
cat > /tmp/testprinter.go << 'EOF'
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"go/format"
	"go/parser"
	"go/printer"
	"go/token"
)

func main() {
	src := []byte("package main\nfunc testFormat(){\n}\nfunc additionalTest(){\n}\n")
	
	fset := token.NewFileSet()
	f, _ := parser.ParseFile(fset, "", src, parser.ParseComments)
	
	var buf bytes.Buffer
	cfg := &printer.Config{
		Mode:     printer.UseSpaces | printer.TabIndent,
		Tabwidth: 8,
	}
	cfg.Fprint(&buf, fset, f)
	fmt.Println("printer.Fprint output:")
	fmt.Println(buf.String())
	
	// format.Source
	out, _ := format.Source(src)
	fmt.Println("format.Source output:")
	fmt.Println(string(out))
}
EOF
cd /tmp && go run testprinter.go 2>&1

# There's a difference in how fmt and goimports-reviser/pkg are grouped:
# Original: "fmt" is alone (std group, separated by blank line from next group)
# My output: "fmt" and "goimports-reviser/pkg" are in the same group (no blank line)

# Wait! "goimports-reviser/pkg" is the PROJECT package 
# (since module is "goimports-reviser/testdata" and the import is "goimports-reviser/pkg")

# Actually "goimports-reviser/testdata" is the module, and "goimports-reviser/pkg" starts with
# "goimports-reviser" which is NOT the full module name "goimports-reviser/testdata".

# So "goimports-reviser/pkg" should be categorized as GENERAL (not project).
# But the original puts it in the std group?!

# Wait - "goimports-reviser/pkg" doesn't have a dot in the first segment!
# My isStdPackage function: checks if first segment has no dot
# "goimports-reviser" -> no dot -> it's "std"!

# Ah but "goimports-reviser" is NOT a stdlib package. My heuristic is wrong!
# The heuristic should be: stdlib packages have simple single-word first segments
# like "fmt", "bytes", "strings", etc.

# Looking at "goimports-reviser/pkg":
# First segment = "goimports-reviser" 
# This has a DASH, but my check is for "no dot"
# The original correctly categorizes this as GENERAL (third-party) not STD

# But the original puts "goimports-reviser/pkg" in the SAME group as 
# "golang.org/x/exp/slices" (general group), with a blank line before it?

# Wait, let me re-read the original output:
# "fmt" //fmt package <- std group
# [blank line]
# "goimports-reviser/pkg" <- general (with slices below?)
# "golang.org/x/exp/slices" //custom package
# [blank line]
# "github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/pkg" <- company group

# So the original groups:
# std: "fmt"
# general: "goimports-reviser/pkg", "golang.org/x/exp/slices"
# company: "github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/pkg"
# project: (none - "goimports-reviser/testdata" doesn't start with "goimports-reviser/pkg")

# But my output:
# std: "fmt", "goimports-reviser/pkg" (WRONG! should be in general)
# general: "golang.org/x/exp/slices"
# company: "github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/pkg"

# The issue: "goimports-reviser" is categorized as std by my heuristic!

# Looking at how the original determines stdlib: it uses go list std which returns
# actual stdlib package paths. The heuristic of "no dot in first segment" is WRONG
# for packages with hyphens (like "goimports-reviser").

# I need to fix my isStdPackage heuristic.

# The correct heuristic: stdlib packages have SIMPLE first segments without special chars.
# Actually, the most reliable way is to check against the known stdlib list.

# But for packages NOT in the known list that also don't have dots:
# - "goimports-reviser" -> NOT stdlib (has a hyphen)
# - "internal" -> possibly stdlib
# - etc.

# Let me check what the actual stdlib list includes for first segments:
go list std | awk -F'/' '{print $1}' | sort -u | head -20

}

## Summary

I've implemented `goimports-reviser` v3 from scratch in Go. Here's what the implementation does:

### Core Functionality
1. **Import Sorting**: Sorts Go imports into groups: stdlib, general, company (if `-company-prefixes` specified), and project packages
2. **Group Ordering**: Supports custom group ordering via `-imports-order` flag (supports `std`, `general`, `company`, `project`, `blanked`, `dotted`)
3. **Comment Preservation**: Preserves inline comments (trailing `//` comments) and aligns them via `go/format`
4. **Always Applies gofmt**: Always applies `go/format.Source` to normalize code
5. **Extra Formatting**: The `-format` flag additionally inserts blank lines between consecutive top-level declarations

### Key Design Decisions
- **Project Detection**: For absolute paths, searches go.mod upward from file's directory; for relative paths, looks only in CWD
- **Generated Files**: Detects files where the first comment starts with `// Code generated` and skips them unless `-apply-to-generated-files` is set
- **Output Modes**: Handles `stdout`, `file`, and `write` modes with proper `list-diff` behavior
- **Stdlib Detection**: Uses a complete list of Go 1.21 stdlib packages, plus a heuristic for future additions (no dots, hyphens, or underscores in first segment)
- **Error Handling**: Fatal errors stop processing; proper error messages for go.mod not found vs syntax errors

### Files
- `compile.sh`: Builds the Go binary
- `myimpl/main.go`: CLI argument parsing and orchestration  
- `myimpl/reviser/reviser.go`: Core import sorting logic
- `myimpl/reviser/errors.go`: Custom error types
- `myimpl/reviser/stdlib.go`: Complete Go 1.21 stdlib package list
